parole.testo: From Middle High German bort (inflected bortes), from Old High German bort (“edge, rim”), from Proto-West Germanic *bord. The modern form in -d and the sense “shelf” are due to influence of cognate Middle Low German bort (inflected bordes), from Old Saxon bord. The shifted t remains in related Borte

From Middle High German barc, from Old High German barug, from Proto-West Germanic *barug. The contemporary vocalism is based on Middle Low German borch, which may be an old variant with zero-grade (compare Old English borg). Cognate with Dutch barg, English barrow.

parole.significato: to compose (a text, almost always poetry)
parole.testo: From Middle High German tihten, from Old High German tihtōn, dihtōn, Proto-West Germanic *dihtōn. The consonantism (d-/t-) was very unstable in early modern German; the voiced onset, which is in line with Middle Low German dichten, has prevailed. Cognate with Dutch dichten, English dight.

From Middle High German ellende, contracted from Old High German elilenti, from Proto-West Germanic *alljas (“other”) + *land (“land”). The modern form with a long vowel is based on Middle Low German elende and/or other regional variants. Today pronounced also with a secondary full vowel in the seco

From Middle High German epfich, epfe, from Old High German epfih, epfi, from Proto-West Germanic *api (“parsley, celery”). The modern consonantism is Central and Low German; compare Middle Low German eppich.

From Middle High German aspe, from Old High German aspa, from Proto-West Germanic *aspu. The modern vocalism is from Middle Low German espe, in which it is generalized from derivatives with umlaut. Cognate with Dutch esp.

parole.significato: to further, foster, advance, encourage, support (promote the development of)
parole.testo: From Middle High German vürdern, from Old High German furdiren, from Proto-West Germanic *furþrijan. Equivalent to archaic fürder (“further”) + -n. parole.significato: young foliage tree of a height between 1 and 2.5 metres
parole.testo: From Middle High German heister, from Old High German *heistar, from Proto-West Germanic *haistr. The word was rare in Middle High German and its modern specialist use chiefly continues cognate Middle Low German heister, hêster (“young tree”).

parole.significato: here; in this place; refers to an environment one is currently in, or to something within reach
parole.testo: From Middle High German hier, from Old High German hier, from Proto-West Germanic *hēr. Cognate with Dutch hier, English here, Swedish här. parole.significato: to scold or nag sharply (stereotypically of older women)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kīben, from Old High German *kīban, from Proto-West Germanic *kīban (“to quarrel”). The modern form with a fricative is of Low and West Central German origin; compare Middle Low German kīven. The original plosive is preserved in the Upper German iterative form kibbeln and kep

parole.significato: clammy, damp, unpleasantly moist (e.g. of fabrics, the air in a room)
parole.testo: From Middle High German klam (“narrow, tight, solid”), from Old High German klam, from or related to Proto-West Germanic *klaimijan (“to smear with clay”). The modern sense is chiefly Central and Low German (Middle Low German klam). Cognate with Dutch klam. Also related with English clammy.

parole.significato: coal (material; either stone coal or charcoal)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kole f alongside commoner kol n, from Old High German kol n, from Proto-West Germanic *kol. The feminine form is chiefly of Central and Low German origin (Middle Low German kōle f). Cognate with Dutch kool f, Danish kul n, English coal.

parole.significato: side, flank (of the body of a person or animal)
parole.testo: From Middle High German lanke, from Old High German hlanka, from Proto-West Germanic *hlanku. The geographic sense is from Middle Low German lanke, from the same Germanic word. Doublet of Flanke, which see.

From Middle High German made, from Old High German mado, from Proto-West Germanic *maþō. Originally a masculine; the feminine gender is of Central and Low German origin (Middle Low German māde f). parole.significato: oar (implement used to propel a boat or ship)
parole.testo: From Middle High German rieme, from Old High German riemo, from Proto-West Germanic *rēmō (“oar”). The word was chiefly restricted to the technical languages of seafaring (Middle Low German rēme) and navigation on the Rhine, in both of which Ruder has indicated primarily the rudder.

From northern Middle High German rētsel, rātsel, from Old High German rādisli (10th c., hapax: ze radislen, Ripuarian), from Proto-West Germanic *rādislī. Equivalent to raten + -sel. The formation was restricted to parts of Central German and was later reinforced by Middle Low German rēdesal, rēdels

From northern Middle High German smouch (13th c.), from Old High German *smouh, from Proto-West Germanic *smauki. parole.significato: smudgy, mucky (covered with sticky dirt or fat residue)
parole.testo: From Middle High German smerwic, smerewic, from Old High German *smerwīg, *smerewīg, from Proto-West Germanic *smerwig, equivalent to Schmiere + -ig. Perhaps also influenced by earlier Middle Low German smērich, which is directly from smēr, cognate of German Schmer.

From Middle High German sëgel, from Old High German segal, from Proto-West Germanic *segl. The word was originally masculine in Upper German, while Central German usage varied. The neuter was later reinforced by cognate Middle Low German sēgel, seil n.

From Middle High German steil, steigel, from Old High German steigal, *steigil, from Proto-West Germanic *staigil (“steep”). 16th century, from archaic stochen (“to stir, stoke”) + -ern (frequentative suffix). Said verb is derived from Proto-West Germanic *stokōn (whence English stoke), possibly through Middle Low German stōken. See stochen for more. Ultimately related with stoßen (“to thrust”) and Stock (“stick”).

16th century, iterative of stäuben, stauben, from Middle High German stöuben, stouben (“to swirl up, raise dust”), from Proto-West Germanic *staubijan, factitive of *steuban (whence stieben). From Middle High German tūchen, touchen, from Old High German *tūhhan – only in firtūhhan (“to sink into oblivion”), intūhhan (“to immerse”) –, from Proto-West Germanic *dūkan. Cognate to Dutch duiken, Swedish dyka. The word had become obsolete in Upper German, but was later reintroduced on the basi

From Middle High German werder, enhanced form of older wert, from Old High German warid, werid, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *wariþ m or n. The suffixed form is northern and was reinforced by Middle Low German werder. Cognate with Dutch waard, Old English waroþ.

From Middle High German zige, from Old High German ziga, from Proto-West Germanic *tigā. Ziege was originally found in Franconian dialects alongside otherwise exclusive Geiß. parole.significato: to look in a searching or cautious way (typically said of animals or of shy, anxious or curious persons)
parole.testo: Formally from Middle High German öugen, ougen, from Old High German ougen, from Proto-West Germanic *augijan, all meaning “to show, let see”. By surface analysis, Auge (“eye”) + -en.
